name: continuation-passing-style
intent: Make the control flow of a computation explicit as data by giving every function an extra parameter - the continuation to apply to its result - so the caller's remaining work travels alongside the call and can be composed, inspected, stored or reinterpreted.
problem: Direct style hides the rest of the computation inside the machine stack: the caller cannot interpose, save, duplicate or run it later, so exceptions, async I/O, backtracking, coroutines and generators all need a separate mechanism bolted onto the language. Any feature that must capture 'what happens next' - undo, retry, timeouts, cooperative multitasking, interpreted targets - ends up reimplementing the same unwinding logic, because the continuation was never a value in the first place.
context: Applies where control must be first-class: interpreters and abstract machines whose order of execution must be independent of the host language, parsers and state machines that must be resumable or replayable, backtracking search, exception and effect handling, async I/O orchestration before async/await existed, and any code generator or compiler pass that needs to reify a program's evaluation context. In a language with first-class, delimited continuations or with async/await, the pattern is usually inherited rather than written - but it is still the shape of the generated code and the right mental model for reading it.
benefits: The rest of the computation becomes a value: it can be stored, duplicated, passed to another function, serialised, or thrown away, which is what makes backtracking, coroutines, generators and interpreters possible at all.

The transformation is a straightforward syntactic rewrite - every tail call gains a continuation argument, every return becomes an application of it - so it can be applied mechanically and proved correct by typing rules rather than by intuition.

It removes the ambient stack: nothing depends on frames being live, so a computation can be suspended, resumed on a different thread, serialised to disk, or executed by a driver loop in constant stack space.
Effect handling composes: success and failure are two ordinary continuations, so exceptions become a two-continuation algebra instead of a language feature with unwinding rules.
Order of evaluation becomes explicit and observable, so an abstract machine built on CPS runs identically whether the host is eager or lazy.
The intermediate program is a first-order data structure after defunctionalisation, which is what makes static analysis and machine simulation tractable.
tradeoffs: Readability collapses: a small direct expression becomes a nest of lambdas, and every variable's use becomes an argument, so the code is much longer and much harder to review.
The transformation is invasive and type-changing: a CPS-converted function has a different type from its source, so a partially converted module does not compose with unconverted callers.
Continuation-passing code allocates a closure per call site in most languages, and the resulting indirect calls defeat inlining and JIT specialisation.
Stack depth is not fixed by the transformation alone: a chain of non-tail calls still nests continuations on the heap, so trampolining or a driver loop is usually required as a second step.
The representation is not the original one: converting back (defunctionalisation in reverse) requires knowing the shape of the continuation set, and general CPS has no useful inverse.
Debugging is harder - the stack trace shows the continuation application rather than the logical call, and the original program's structure has to be recovered by hand.

One-shot versus multi-shot semantics is a real design fork: a plain function continuation can be called once safely, but code that assumes re-entry (as in a loop) changes meaning under a language whose continuations are multi-shot.
quality_attributes_note: Extensibility is high because the continuation is an ordinary value any new control feature can be built from; maintainability and simplicity are low because the transformation multiplies nesting and length. Type safety stays high - CPS-converted programs are usually given an answer-type-indexed type, which catches missing and duplicated continuations at compile time.

participants.responsibility: Takes its ordinary arguments plus a continuation, and instead of returning a value calls the continuation with it.
participants.notes: Its type changes from A -> B to A -> (B -> R) -> R; that type change is the whole point.

participants.responsibility: The caller's remaining computation as a function of the result.
participants.notes: Often an inline lambda at the call site; that is what makes the transformed code hard to read.

participants.responsibility: Supplies the continuation, typically as an anonymous function wrapping the rest of its own body.
participants.notes: Every call becomes a call wrapped in a lambda - this is where the nesting comes from.

participants.responsibility: Supplied once at the entry point to return the value to the original caller.
participants.notes: ‖e‖ = λk. k(e): the transformed program still needs a place to start.

participants.responsibility: Replaces the continuation closures with a finite sum type and one apply function, yielding a first-order program.
participants.notes: The step that makes the CPS program analysable and machine-executable.

participants.responsibility: Interprets the returned steps when the CPS program is not tail-recursive.
participants.notes: Without it the transformation relocates stack growth from frames to the heap.

use_cases: Language interpreters: Reynolds' CPS-plus-defunctionalisation turns a direct-style interpreter into an abstract machine whose execution order does not depend on the host's eagerness - the foundational use.
Backtracking search, where a success continuation and a failure continuation are two ordinary values and the choice of which to invoke becomes data.
Exception and effect handling modelled as a (B -> R) -> (E -> R) -> R pair, giving an algebra that composes instead of a runtime unwinding rule.
Async I/O before the language had it: Node's original callback machinery and Python's pre-async generators are CPS in all but name.
Compiler passes that reify a program's evaluation context - accumulating parameters, reassociating folds, and the fast-reverse transformation are all applications of the same associativity argument.
Serialization and resumption of computations: a continuation value can be written down and replayed, which is what makes a resumable parser or a persisted workflow possible.
Async/await and Kotlin suspend functions as they are actually compiled: a stackless coroutine is a CPS transformation into a state machine, and reading generated code requires knowing this.
avoid_when: The language has async/await, exceptions or generators already - use those; hand-rolling CPS re-implements the runtime and loses the compiler's state-machine layout.
The computation is direct-style recursion with shallow depth and no need to interpose - a normal call is faster, shorter and debuggable.
The code is going to be read and modified by people who did not write the transformation; CPS in ordinary application code is a maintenance liability.
The continuation would be a lambda per call in a hot path - the closure allocation and the lost inlining usually cost more than the benefit.
You only need to interpose on one narrow call, not on the whole control flow: a callback, a strategy or a decorator is the smaller and clearer tool.
pitfalls: Converting only the tail of a program: a partially converted module keeps both conventions, and the boundary between them is where the bugs live.
Forgetting that non-tail calls nest continuations on the heap: CPS alone does not give constant stack space - trampolining or an explicit stack is required as well.

Confusing the continuation parameter with a callback that may be called later or more than once: under single-shot semantics, storing and re-invoking one is a logic error that no type system catches by default.
Using the last argument for the continuation and then partially applying, which changes evaluation order and can turn an eager computation into a deferred one that runs at an unexpected time.
Dropping the distinction between the success and failure continuation, which loses the exception path entirely and produces code that returns a default value where it should have signalled failure.

Trusting that defunctionalisation is cheap: it is a whole-program transformation, so a single un-converted function called through the apply function leaves a residual higher-order value that defeats the point.

related_patterns_notes.trampoline: The direct companion. CPS makes control explicit as a value; trampolining is the driver loop that executes those values in constant stack space. The trampoline record's own source list and related-patterns notes already name continuation-passing-style as the technique it protects, so the two belong together.
related_patterns_notes.generator: A generator is the special case where the continuation is the consumer's 'give me the next element' request - CPS made multi-shot by allowing the continuation to be re-entered on each iteration.
related_patterns_notes.interpreter-as-data: CPS plus defunctionalisation is exactly how an interpreter becomes a data structure; interpreter-as-data is the result of that pair of transformations.
related_patterns_notes.monad: A monad's bind is a composition of continuations in disguise: the continuation of a monadic chain is the remaining binds, which is why monad transformers and CPS-constructed interpreters are the same idea at two levels.
related_patterns_notes.tail-recursion: CPS is how a tail call is guaranteed - once the call is in tail position with an accumulator, the continuation never returns - which is why the two are so often introduced together.
related_patterns_notes.command: Both make 'what to do next' an explicit value that can be queued, stored or dispatched elsewhere; a command is the object-flavoured continuation.
related_patterns_notes.interpreter: The classic pairing. A direct-style interpreter transformed by CPS and defunctionalisation becomes an abstract machine: the continuation is the machine's state, which is why CPS and interpreter-as-data share this record's sources.
related_patterns_notes.state: A state monad is CPS with the continuation specialised to one shape: read the state, run the action, write it back. Hand-rolled CPS is more general but the monad is the readable version when only state threading is needed.
related_patterns_notes.async-method-invocation: POSA's return-address pattern: instead of a blocking call, the invoker supplies a continuation object to be invoked on completion - the object-flavoured form of exactly the same 'pass the rest of the computation along' idea.

anti_patterns: Hand-writing CPS in a language with async/await, and thereby losing the compiler-generated state machine, the cancellation support and the readable stack traces.
CPS with a trampoline inside the continuation itself - double-driving the machine and hiding which layer actually controls the stack.
Writing CPS by hand for a computation whose depth is small and known, spending readability on a problem recursion does not have.
Using a general recursion driver (defunctionalisation) when defunctionalising only the continuations would do - the whole-program version bloats the representation for nothing.
Assuming continuations are multi-shot because your tests only call them once; re-entrant code then breaks under a language whose continuation semantics differ.
Passing the continuation as the first argument instead of the last, and losing the left-to-right evaluation order the standard transformation is defined to preserve.
Mixing CPS with direct style inside one function so that neither convention can be read consistently.
design_principles: Make the control explicit: the continuation is the value, and any feature that needs to interpose operates on it.
One convention per module: a half-converted program is worse than either convention alone.
Separate the transformation from the logic: the CPS rewrite should be mechanical, so the algorithm inside it stays readable.
Pair with an explicit stack discipline: constant stack space is a property of the driver, not of CPS alone.
Type the answer: the continuation's result type is what makes duplicated and dropped continuations compile errors.
best_practices: Use the host language's CPS when it has one - async functions in JavaScript, suspend functions in Kotlin, generators in Python - and treat the transformation as what it is: a compilation strategy.
Add a step budget or stack limit to a CPS interpreter that processes untrusted input, because constant stack space comes from the driver, not from the transformation.
Keep the CPS transformation in a separate pass or module so the algorithm can still be read and tested in direct style.
Document whether the continuation is one-shot or multi-shot at every boundary where it escapes the call site.
Name the continuation parameters consistently and put them last, so a reader can mentally delete the trailing lambda and recover the direct-style program.
Test the interpreter against a direct-style reference implementation on the same inputs; agreement is the practical correctness oracle.
Prefer a trampoline driver over recursion for CPS code that recurses on data depth, and measure - the closure allocation per step is real.
Do not convert code that no one needs to interpose on; the cost is paid by every future reader.
sources: Jeremy Gibbons, 'Continuation-Passing Style, Defunctionalization, Accumulations, and Associativity' (Oxford) - Reynolds' CPS + defunctionalisation recipe for turning a direct-style interpreter into an abstract machine, and the associativity argument that drives the later transformations. https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/jeremy.gibbons/publications/continued.pdf

Danvy and Pfenning, 'A Functional Correspondence between Evaluations and Deduction' / lecture notes on CPS transformation - the definition of ‖e‖K and the claim/value split that makes evaluation order explicit. https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~fp/courses/15417-s25/lectures/20-cps.pdf

Xavier Leroy, 'Functional programming languages - Part III: program transformations' (typing course, Radboud University) - the closure-conversion and defunctionalisation definitions, the CPS conversion table for core constructs, and the call-with-current-continuation semantics. http://cs.ru.nl/~freek/courses/tt-2017/papers/transformations.pdf

Olivier Danvy, 'Defunctionalization at Work' (TOPLAS) - why first-order programs are produced by enumerating the function abstractions of a whole program and dispatching in one apply function. https://www.cs.tufts.edu/~nr/cs257/archive/olivier-danvy/defunc.pdf
